description: Compute the true area centroid of a coordinate polygon with Polygon Centroid From Coordinates — the balance point, not the box middle. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the Midtown Manhattan test polygon (1.742 km² over four corners) balances at 40.7640, −73.9777 — while an L-shaped field's centroid can sit outside the field entirely, in the neighbour's hedge.
quick_answer: Polygon Centroid From Coordinates computes the area centroid — the balance point — of a polygon given by latitude/longitude corners, using the area-weighted centroid formula. Paste the corners in boundary order and read the centre point: the spot where the shape would balance, for labels, anchors and representative points.

body.t: The Manhattan test rectangle balances at its exact middle, 40.7640, −73.9777 — the formula bowing to the obvious when the shape is obvious.

An L-shaped polygon's centroid falls in the crook of the L — sometimes on land the polygon does not contain. It is a balance point, not a promise of membership; label placement sometimes prefers a point-on-surface instead.

faq: How is this different from averaging the corners?
Averaging corners weights places where you happened to add points. The area centroid weights land — dense corner clusters along one fence stop dragging the 'centre' toward themselves.
Can the centroid fall outside the polygon?
Yes, for concave (C, L, U) shapes — it is a balance point in the mathematical sense. If your use needs an inside point, a point-on-surface method is the right tool.
The formula handles either direction; the reported point is the same. Order along the boundary, however, is essential — scrambled corners break both shape and centre.

This tool weights by area alone. Population-weighted centres are a different instrument (the meeting-point family computes people-weighted centres).
The formula runs on a local projection at the polygon's latitude — at district scales the distinction from geodesic truth is beneath notice.
